transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Hurricane NOLO is moving toward Hawaii, with its outer bands already reaching the Big Island
and forecasters warning of potentially catastrophic flooding.
farther east, category 4 hurricane polo, with maximum sustained winds of 145 mph, is threatening
Baja California Sur, where a hurricane watch is in effect.
The Pacific's already seen an extremely active hurricane season, with climate scientists pointing
to the powerful Super El Nino pattern as a major factor.
NPR's Ava Berger has more.
There have been no full-blown hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean yet this season.
It's the first time that has happened in more than a century.
It's the exact opposite for the Pacific Ocean.
The Pacific has already seen 18 hurricanes, more than the average, and these storms can
be really strong. Gabriel Vecchi, a professor of geosciences at Princeton University, said
hurricane polo increased faster than any hurricane he's ever seen.
It's a tale of two basins, the Pacific incredibly active and the North Atlantic incredibly inactive.
Vecchi and other climate scientists point to a super strong El Nino to explain the weather.
This natural pattern occurs every few years and tends to suppress hurricanes in the Atlantic
while fueling more storms in the Pacific.
Ava Berger, NPR News.
Investors bought stocks and dumped bonds this week.
As NPR's Scott Horsley reports, a sell-off in the bond market pushed mortgage rates to
their highest level since the beginning of last year.
Long-term Treasury yields jumped again this week as investors demand a bigger return to
lend money for the government in the face of stubborn inflation.
The yield on 10-year Treasuries climbed to the highest level in two decades.
Average mortgage rates, which tend to follow Treasury yields, rose to just over 7 percent.
Mortgage rates had briefly dropped below 6 percent just before the U.S. launched its
war with Iran and triggered a spike in energy prices.
Today's higher borrowing costs have been a drag on the housing market.
Sales of existing homes in August were the slowest in more than a year.
For the week, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose three-tenths of a percent, the S&P 500
index climbed 1.2 percent, and the NASDAQ jumped more than 2 percent.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
In France, scores of people turned out in Paris for Pope Leo's outdoor Mass today.
The Vatican says more than 600,000 people registered for the Mass and...
Leo greeted people as he rode in his popemobile along a parade during the Champs-Elysees, heading
to the place where Mass was held, this amid tight security.
It's the first papal visit in 18 years, and it's a sign of the Catholic Church's continuing
appeal in a country now officially secular but once strongly Catholic.
Leo was on a four-day visit to France starting yesterday with a prayer in the newly restored
Notre Dame Cathedral.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
For the third time, the Supreme Court blocked a congressional map in Missouri in a redistricting
case that could help determine control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
The GOP-friendly map was meant to help Republicans get another seat in the House.
The court's order requires the state to use the same voting districts used in 2022 and
2024, warning that changing the maps now would cause "electoral chaos," this after a week
of conflicting rulings in state and federal courts.
In Brazil, with just over a week left before national elections, the president has ordered
a ban on online betting.
The move, the leader says, is for the health and welfare of families who are falling deeper
into debt in the South American country, and pierce Carrie Khan has more.
Online gambling has exploded in Brazil in recent years, and so has personal debt, as
well as gambling addictions and suicides, according to a recent national study.
In signing the banning order, President Luis Anacio Lula da Silva said his decision was
hard and drastic but necessary.
Lula is locked in a tough re-election campaign with the son of former right-wing President
Jair Bolsonaro.
Flavio Bolsonaro, who is polling at a statistical tie with Lula for the presidency, criticized
the ban as a "electoral measure."
Brazil Central Bank estimates that Brazilians spend nearly $6 billion a month on gambling.
Brazil's soccer clubs, however, say without the advertising from online betting houses,
their clubs could close.
Carrie Khan, NPR News, Rio de Janeiro.
And I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.
